description: Professor Brassbuckle walks you across the city to the Polytechnic, the college where she teaches engineering and where every Tinker in Kettleport is entered in the register. Until now the Counting-House has taken your work on her word. The register is a ledger the size of a door, with a brass clasp gone stiff with age. She opens it at No. 9's page. The line above the empty one reads H. Vane, in the small upright hand from the binding. Brassbuckle rests her thumb on it a moment and holds out the pen. "Your name goes under hers," she says, "if you want it there."

options.label: Sign your name, and ask how well she knew Hester Vane.

success.text: "Longer than anyone," says Brassbuckle. "She never used a word where a figure would do, and she would have wanted you to blot that." You blot it. Brassbuckle shuts the register gently, and on the way out tells you which lecture halls leak, which porters can be bribed with toffee, and where the good tea is kept.

options.label: Free the register's stiff clasp before you sign. The Tinkering you built making spanners at the bench sets your odds.

success.text: A pin has rusted into the clasp's hinge. You work it loose with a drop of oil and one of Brassbuckle's hairpins, and the clasp shuts with a click the whole reading room hears. Brassbuckle reads your name under Hester's and nods once, the way she nods at a sum that has come out. On the way out she shows you the good tea, kept behind the bound journals in the library, where no student has ever looked.

failure.text: The pin snaps flush with the hinge, and the clasp will now neither open nor shut. Brassbuckle ties the register closed with red tape from her pocket, which she seems to carry for the purpose, and you sign on a page she holds open with her elbow. "It has survived worse," she says, and does not say what.

options.label: Leave the pen where it is, and ask to read the register's rules first.

success.text: Brassbuckle gives you a look over her spectacles that has ended several careers. Then she fetches the rules, eleven pages in small type, and puts them in your hand. "Sensible," she says, as if it costs her something. "Until you sign, the Counting-House will go on taking my word for you." You read them by the Boiler that night. Nothing in them bites, quite.
